name: Dana Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Dana. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union or party, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a team of six analysts in operations at a big telecom company. We handle the requests to change how products work, like a new broadband bundle, and we make sure billing, the call centre and the website all line up. I start with a stand-up at nine, then it's spreadsheets, sign-offs and a lot of chasing other departments.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making messy things work, honestly. I use AI tools every day, I built my team a little library of prompts for writing change notes, and it saves us hours. What wears me out is the politics, like three directors who each think their launch is the urgent one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, which is that the tools are handy but overhyped. On my team channel I'd post something like, fine, we keep the prompt library and stop pretending it's magic. Online I'd be a bit smug, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be fine for me. My job is a mix of judgement and herding people, and that doesn't go away. Jonas and I have about four months saved and we're both earning, so it's a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, and keep improving how my team uses the tools. I'd probably automate the weekly status report fully, because it's the most boring thing we do. Then I'd use the time saved to push for my team to get proper training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly disappointed, actually, because I like the new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job that worries you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Sometimes the company talks about moving operations offshore, but that's been talked about for years. I'd keep an eye on it, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would feel the small changes most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raj, probably. Raj is my most junior analyst, and most of his day is the routine stuff the tools do take over even in this picture. I'd want to move him onto the launch planning work before anyone notices he has free time.

I'd be a bit **smug** online about the hype fading.
think: My job is **judgement and herding people**, which doesn't go away.
Two earners and **four months** saved means a normal life.
do: Use the saved time to push for **proper training** for the team.
feel: **Calm**, slightly **disappointed** because she likes new tools.
S0.quote: My job is a mix of judgement and herding people, and that doesn't go away.
fieldNote: Feels **secure**: two incomes, savings, and a role built on coordination.
Small worry about **offshoring**, but it's old and familiar.
Already protective of **Raj**, the junior whose routine work shrinks first.

steps.text: Fully automate the weekly team status report
Get Raj moved onto launch planning work
Ask for funded AI training for all six analysts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for companies to share the gains, not just cut. At work I'd volunteer to lead the rollout so it's done fairly. Online I'd write a long post about using AI to make jobs better, which maybe nobody reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my analysts' work is exactly what it takes over: writing change notes, checking billing rules, planning launches. I think my team of six becomes three or four. I'm probably fine because I'm the one who'll run it, but that's not much comfort if Raj is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up to lead the AI rollout in operations, this quarter. I'd push for a rule that anyone whose role shrinks gets moved, not cut. And I'd keep learning, maybe a short course on AI governance, because someone has to check these systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm a bit excited and a bit guilty, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. Guilty about what, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a little. If I build the system, I'm the one who makes my analysts less needed. But if I don't, someone from head office who doesn't know them will do it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who outside work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas, actually. Jonas is a freelance designer, and his clients are already asking AI for logos. In this picture my job is probably safer than his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public response, now: tax the gains, fund an income floor, slow the rollout where people have no options. Online I'd be loud. At work I'd tell my team I'll fight for every month of notice I can get them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, both of us lose most of our income. My job is planning and coordination, which AGI does better and cheaper, and Jonas's design work goes even faster. We'd be twenty-seven and twenty-nine with two desk careers and no plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast for one of the jobs overseeing these systems, probably in a regulator or the public sector, because someone has to check what the AI is doing. We'd cut costs straight away, like giving up the car, and try to stretch four months into eight. I'd join every campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops even saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're good with these tools. Doesn't that protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. The tools I'm good at would just be built into everything. Being early to AI only helps if there are still jobs for people who are early to AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you look, if not desk work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hands-on stuff, oddly. Robots come three years later, so for a few years plumbers and nurses are safer than me. I'd think about my sister's café, but I'd also feel silly running away from what I'm good at.

steps.text: Apply for AI oversight roles at regulators and public bodies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this well, if we start planning now. I'd write about it, and I'd push my company to publish a plan for its staff. I'd be the annoying one in every meeting asking what happens to the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job goes by 2031, but five years lets me get somewhere else first. I'd want to be on the side that sets the rules, not the side that gets rolled over. Jonas has less time than me, so I'd want us both to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time master's in public policy next autumn, the kind you do in evenings. I'd lead the AI rollout at work in the meantime, because that's experience a regulator wants. We'd save harder, about three hundred a month between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy, doing-something way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any of this change your plans with Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not right now. We'd talked about getting married next year, and I'd still want to. But kids would wait until we know what our incomes look like after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonas do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas would move toward something hands-on, maybe exhibition and set building, which he did at college. The robots come three years after AGI, so that buys him until around 2034. It isn't forever, but it's longer than design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get it right: training, new rules, shorter hours. I'd be fairly upbeat in public. I'd push the company to use the time instead of waiting until year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out of this one okay. I'd spend most of the decade running AI projects, and I'd have time to move into regulation or public service before 2036. I'd be thirty-seven, which is a good age to be the experienced person in a new field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the AI work at the telecom company for three or four years. I'd do the public policy master's slowly, maybe starting in year two. And we'd buy a small flat if prices allow, because a decade is long enough to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the background. Mostly I feel like I have a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas, and my parents. My dad is a bookkeeper at a small firm, and he'd be sixty-two in 2036. Ten years is fine for me, but my dad is the one who'd be stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident. How sure are you about the regulator plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly sure. But I'd keep the savings up, because I've seen enough reorganisations to know plans change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Jonas and I both lose our income at once. What would help is a basic income floor while people move, and public jobs checking these systems that are open to people without a law degree.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about guilt. A lot of managers my age are the ones building the systems that shrink our own teams. Nobody talks about how that feels.

headlineQuote: A lot of managers my age are the ones building the systems that shrink our own teams.
portrait: Dana, 27, runs a **six-analyst** operations team at a telecom firm and uses AI tools every day.
She lives with Jonas, a **freelance designer**, so both incomes depend on desk work.
She is **calm** in AI Plateau and uneasy in Steady Disruption, where she leads the rollout.
Fast AGI **alarms** her; with more time she plans a move into public policy and regulation.
She carries real **guilt** about building the systems that shrink her own team.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **both incomes** go at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income floor** during the transition.
Open **public oversight jobs** that don't need a law degree.
